questions.q: What does the psalmist tell the people to do to God?
questions.a: He tells them to shout joyfully to God, their strength, and to shout out to the God of Jacob.

questions.q: What instruments do the psalmist tell the people to use as they raise a song?
questions.a: The psalmist tells the people to play tambourines, harps, and lyres.

questions.q: When should the people blow the shofar?
questions.a: They should blow it at the new moon and at the full moon for the day of their festival.

questions.q: Who gave these commands for Israel?
questions.a: The God of Jacob gave these commands for Israel.

questions.q: What did God tell their ancestors to observe?
questions.a: He told their ancestors to observe these things when he delivered them from slavery in the land of Egypt.

questions.q: What did God remove from the shoulder of the people?
questions.a: He removed the burden from their shoulder, and their hands no longer had to carry heavy baskets full of bricks.

questions.q: What happened when the people called out in their distress?
questions.a: God delivered them and answered them from the secret place of thunder, and he tested them at the waters of Meribah.

questions.q: What did God say about strange gods?
questions.a: God said there must be no strange god among Israel, and they must not bow down to any god that other nations worship.

questions.q: What does Yahweh say he did for Israel?
questions.a: He brought them up from slavery in the land of Egypt.

questions.q: What promise did God make to the Israelites?
questions.a: He promised them that if they depended on him, that he would provide everything they needed.

questions.q: What did Yahweh’s people, Israel, not do?
questions.a: They did not listen to Yahweh’s voice, and Israel did not submit to him.

questions.q: What did Yahweh do when his people refused to listen to him?
questions.a: He sent them away in the stubbornness of their heart, and they walked in their own counsels.

questions.q: What does Yahweh long for his people to do?
questions.a: Yahweh wants his people to listen to him and walk in his ways.

questions.q: What would Yahweh do if his people would listen to him and walk in his ways?
questions.a: He would easily subdue their enemies and turn his hand against their adversaries.

questions.q: According to Yahweh, what would happen to those who hate him?
questions.a: They would cringe before him, but the Israelites would always prosper.

questions.q: What does Yahweh say he would do for Israel?
questions.a: Yahweh would feed them with the fat of the wheat and satisfy them with honey from the rock.

commentary.text: God is praised for what he has done for his people.

Verses 1–7 All the worship we can render to the Lord is beneath his excellences, and our obligations to him, especially in our redemption from sin and wrath. What God had done on Israel's behalf, was kept in remembrance by public solemnities. To make a deliverance appear more gracious, more glorious, it is good to observe all that makes the trouble we are delivered from appear more grievous. We ought never to forget the base and ruinous drudgery to which Satan, our oppressor, brought us. But when, in distress of conscience, we are led to cry for deliverance, the Lord answers our prayers, and sets us at liberty. Convictions of sin, and trials by affliction, prove his regard to his people. If the Jews, on their solemn feast-days, were thus to call to mind their redemption out of Egypt, much more ought we, on the Christian sabbath, to call to mind a more glorious redemption, wrought out for us by our Lord Jesus Christ, from worse bondage.

We cannot look for too little from the creature, nor too much from the Creator. We may have enough from God, if we pray for it in faith. All the wickedness of the world is owing to man's wilfulness. People are not religious, because they will not be so. God is not the Author of their sin, he leaves them to the lusts of their own hearts, and the counsels of their own heads; if they do not well, the blame must be upon themselves. The Lord is unwilling that any should perish. What enemies sinners are to themselves! It is sin that makes our troubles long, and our salvation slow. Upon the same conditions of faith and obedience, do Christians hold those spiritual and eternal good things, which the pleasant fields and fertile hills of Canaan showed forth. Christ is the Bread of life; he is the Rock of salvation, and his promises are as honey to pious minds. But those who reject him as their Lord and Master, must also lose him as their Saviour and their reward.
